title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced one shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini and evaluated that candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We revise presentation to (1) give a compact, formal definition of the binary outcome used in the confirmatory test with a representative artifact-grounded example, (2) provide a concise nearest-work comparison highlighting methodological differences, and (3) tighten experimental interpretation and concrete design recommendations for future confirmatory studies where generators produce more invalid candidates.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs can translate operator intent into device commands, improving NetOps throughput. Yet syntactically plausible commands may violate workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without required shutdown, or performing an unsafe uplink switchover), yielding semantic failures only visible in closed-loop execution. Prior tool papers and benchmarks therefore recommend integrating verification, emulation, or veto layers so that generated candidates are validated before enactment. Measuring the marginal benefit of such guarded pipelines requires experimental designs that separate generator variability from validator/repair efficacy. We executed a preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that fixes the generator output and compares the same candidate in (a) an LLM-only suggestion scoring lane (baseline) and (b) an executable generate→validate→repair lane (guarded). Our central confirmatory question was: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) isolating validator/repair marginal effects under a shared-generation design; (2) a compact formalization of the binary pass/fail outcome and a representative artifact-grounded example; (3) an explicit nearest-work comparison showing where this validator-focused lens differs from generator-focused studies; and (4) concrete methodological recommendations for follow-up confirmatory designs when generators produce few invalid candidates.
sections.related_work: Executable emulation and closed-loop NetOps benchmarks establish that text-level correctness alone can miss sequencing and stateful errors; recent efforts (NetConfArena and similar executable benchmarks) run generated configurations in emulated network states to reveal make-before-break, group-availability, and ordered-operation failures. A parallel literature proposes tool-augmented agentic architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, translation-to-formal-model, generate→validate→repair) to reduce operational risk. Representative prior works used independently drawn generator outputs or focused on generator diagnostics, producing measurements that confound generator variance with verifier effects; by contrast our study uses a shared-generation paired design to isolate validator/repair effects on identical candidates. Nearest-work comparison (compact): - Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair (Protogeros et al., arXiv 2604.22513): generator-focused repair benchmark; typically independent generation per condition and multiple models. Difference: independent-generation lens versus our shared-candidate, validator-marginal lens. - NetConfArena / executable-benchmark suites (NetConfArena, arXiv 2608.23179): closed-loop emulation to reveal semantic failures. Difference: similar use of emulation, but published suites often evaluate generator families rather than isolating validator marginal effects with a paired shared-candidate protocol. - Aether: Agentic AI + Digital Twin (arXiv 2604.18233): digital-twin validation architectures emphasizing translation to formal models. Difference: architectural position paper and prototype; our contribution is a preregistered paired experiment measuring a narrowly defined marginal effect. - MeshAgent (Zhou et al., 2025): engineering prototype for reliable LLM-driven network management. Difference: system-level prototype and multi-component evaluation; our work presents an explicit statistical confirmatory design with complete execution accounting. This study complements those streams by providing a validator-focused experimental lens and by documenting operational artifacts and deterministic reconciliation for reproducible failure analysis.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 (preregistration_sha256 = 0bfc96e9afceed579f04a06dcbad2387ee4acca970559d9a4faa165893f4fe50) and specified a paired binary confirmatory design with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks partitioned deterministically into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine, 40 tasks each). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the prespecified test was the exact two-sided McNemar. A bootstrap-percentile 95% CI used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729. The preregistration also fixed a repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), deterministic reset controls, contamination rules, and sensitivity analyses.

Task generation and shared-candidate design. Tasks were deterministically generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task payload includes initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, and a structured required_sequence (canonical ordered operations) so the validator can apply structured checks. To isolate validator/repair marginal effects we used a single shared initial candidate per task: one generation call (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini) produced the candidate that was scored in both baseline and guarded conditions. Execution accounting shows model_calls_used = 120 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}.

Formal outcome definition and scoring rule (compact). To make the binary label used in the McNemar test explicit: for every episode (baseline and guarded) the deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0) executed the candidate in emulated state and emitted a structured validator_trace containing validation_after.valid (boolean) and violation_count (integer). The binary pass/fail label used in the confirmatory test was defined a priori as: PASS if validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true AND validator_trace.violation_count == 0; FAIL otherwise. Repair application semantics: in the guarded lane only, when violation_count > 0 the preregistered repair policy could invoke at most one repair iteration; archived repair prompts/traces would be stored. Representative artifact-grounded example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json shows normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and validator_trace.violation_count = 0, therefore label = PASS for the baseline episode of pair-000001.

Instrumentation and contamination controls. The harness enforced deterministic emulator resets (container images + deterministic seeds) between tasks; contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection, cross-condition cache-key reuse) were applied. Exclusion and missingness rules were prespecified; in this run no technical/instrumentation exclusions occurred. Deterministic_reconciliation checked episode accounting, provider-call audits, and pair accounting for consistency.

Statistical analysis. Primary test: exact two-sided McNemar on paired PASS/FAIL labels; report exact p-value and the paired-success-rate difference estimate with a bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Secondary endpoints (preregistered but vacuous here because no repairs occurred) included mean model calls per successful task and incidence of repair iterations.

sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The shared-generation paired design isolates validator/repair marginal effects by fixing generator variability. The empirical consequence in this task bank and under the frozen prompt/model configuration was that the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator in all 120 pairs; therefore the guarded subsystem had no opportunity to exercise repair and could not reduce semantic failures relative to baseline. The observed exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00] are direct statistical expressions of this ceiling behavior under the preregistered resampling scheme (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729).

Design trade-offs and concrete recommendations. The shared-candidate design increases internal validity for isolating validator effects but risks under-exercising repair when a generator is well-calibrated for the selected task bank. Based on the archived task_manifest difficulty fields (dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level) and the recorded absence of repairs, we recommend for future confirmatory studies: (1) allow independent generator draws per condition (or blocked randomization) to expose generator variance that the guard might mitigate, (2) target tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count to increase generator-induced violation probability, (3) include controlled prompt perturbations on prespecified subsets to raise error incidence while preserving preplanned pairings for sensitivity checks, and (4) consider an exploratory arm with an expanded repair budget (≥1 iteration) to measure repair convergence behavior. These recommendations are implementable using the archived task_manifest difficulty metadata without changing the validator semantics.

Operational implications and auditability. Even when unused, an executable validator that emits structured traces (validation verdicts, touched fields, parsed command counts, and explicit rule-check failures) supports operator auditability and post-hoc analysis. The archived artifacts demonstrate end-to-end instrumented accounting (provider-call audits, scoring traces, deterministic reconciliation) that can underpin operator explanations and third-party audits in deployments where generators sometimes err.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity: limited by the validator's policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads; the validator enforces declared required_sequence and workflow policies but does not emulate all vendor-specific behaviors or partial-observability telemetry. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumed baseline failure ≈0.40; observed baseline = 0.00 violates that assumption and renders the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted absolute reduction of 0.15.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The run documents a ceiling for this curated synthetic task bank and demonstrates that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. The principal contribution is methodological: we show how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects, and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, deterministic reconciliation) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. Archived artifacts support follow-up runs that relax shared-generation constraints, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for the preregistered effect size.
